abstract:
Industrial computational fluid dynamics (CFD) becomes costly when complex geometries, long transients and coupled physics must be evaluated across large design spaces. We introduce FastAgent, a physics-aware campaign controller built around FastFluent, a lightweight numerical engine for rapid physical screening. FastFluent supplies stage-specific fields and diagnostics; FastAgent allocates physical models, numerical resolution and simulation horizons by the active quantities of interest (QoIs), while returned Fluent discrepancies update subsequent decisions. Across six public CFD benchmark campaigns, the framework reduces normalised worst-QoI error by 5.68–99.14% and accelerates decision-relevant computation by factors of 1.53–15.36 relative to a matched Generic Agent control.

Applied to high-pressure steam dewaxing in investment casting, FastAgent identifies nonuniform condensation heating as the dominant startup mechanism and separates rapid risk-window localisation from high-fidelity melt-completion confirmation. The rapid route requires 81.39% fewer cell-time updates than a fine-grid, small-time-step reference. Structural analysis localises fracture at the observed blade edge. Screening 131,072 outlet layouts and selectively evaluating candidates with Fluent and Abaqus identifies Sparse-6, which reduces simulated crack opening by 96.0% and connected crack extent by 66.7% relative to the Original design. These results demonstrate how rapid numerical evidence and adaptive fidelity control connect large CFD search spaces to mechanism-guided industrial design.

sections.body: The introduction argues that CFD campaigns need fidelity chosen per quantity of interest, because existing CFD agents mostly automate prescribed solver workflows. It introduces FastAgent, which treats the physical model, numerical resolution and simulation horizon as QoI-dependent decisions, and FastFluent, a lightweight engine that brings lattice-Boltzmann flow calculations, conservative finite-volume balances and reduced-order thermal phase-change screening into one representation. Steam dewaxing is the test case, with 17 binary outlet positions generating 131,072 layouts. The section reports that the selected Sparse-6 design reduces simulated crack opening by 96.0% relative to the Original design. It states three contributions: a purpose-built rapid engine, QoI-specific control across process stages, and discrepancy-updated design selection.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: FastAgent couples a rapid physics engine with QoI-aware fidelity control and discrepancy feedback for industrial CFD campaigns.

sections.body: Six public benchmark campaigns test numerical correction, transient diagnosis, QoI transfer, full-field confirmation, discrepancy-driven refinement and adaptive stopping. Representative errors and diagnostic deviations remain below 1%, with measured speedups of 1.28–2.65 against fixed Fluent schedules. In matched-evidence replay, FastAgent satisfied all stagewise criteria in six campaigns, compared with five for the Generic Agent (19/19 versus 18/19 prescribed actions). Relative to the Generic Agent workflow, normalised worst-QoI error falls by 5.68–99.14% and decision-relevant computation accelerates by factors of 1.53–15.36. The laminar-channel values are lower bounds, and the cylinder comparisons begin from a shared 4.0 s checkpoint.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Across six public benchmark campaigns, FastAgent cut worst-QoI error by 5.68–99.14% and accelerated computation by factors of 1.53–15.36 versus a Generic Agent control.

sections.body: Methods define a campaign as geometry, physical assumptions, candidate parameters, target QoIs and a budget. FastAgent checks completeness, physical admissibility, numerical reliability and QoI coverage in that order. FastFluent uses lattice-Boltzmann flow on regular domains, conservative finite-volume balances on unstructured domains and a reduced-order thermal phase-change model for full-cycle dewaxing. Validation takes worst-QoI error as the maximum normalised deviation, with reductions and speedups measured against a matched Generic Agent control. Structural analysis distributes wax expansion over 16 shell regions using wax compressibility and shell compliance. Layout selection weights fracture severity with 0.40, 0.25, 0.20 and 0.15. Global and local calculations remained quasi-static, and a 35/45 mm domain comparison gave essentially unchanged crack timing and opening.
sections.heading: Methods
sections.headline: The methods define the campaign policy, FastFluent governing formulations, error metrics and fracture-based layout screening.

sections.body: The conclusions restate that FastAgent combines FastFluent screening, QoI-dependent fidelity control and discrepancy-updated design selection, with the physical model, numerical resolution and simulation horizon adapting to each decision. Across six public CFD benchmark campaigns, normalised worst-QoI error falls by 5.68–99.14% and decision-relevant computation accelerates by factors of 1.53–15.36 relative to a matched Generic Agent control. For steam dewaxing, the rapid route localises the full-cycle risk window using 81.39% fewer cell-time updates than the fine-grid, small-time-step reference, while Fluent confirms melt completion. Screening 131,072 layouts, followed by selective Fluent and Abaqus evaluation, identifies Sparse-6, which reduces simulated crack opening by 96.0% and connected crack extent by 66.7% relative to the Original design.
sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.headline: FastAgent identifies Sparse-6, which cuts simulated crack opening by 96.0% and connected crack extent by 66.7% versus the Original design.
